title: Leeds and Rangers co-owner jailed after prostitution arrest
description: The 49ers were part of the US consortium who took control of Rangers last year but York is not involved in the day-to-day running of the club.Rangers
body: The 49ers were part of the US consortium who took control of Rangers last year but York is not involved in the day-to-day running of the club.Rangers and Leeds have both said they will not be commenting. The 49ers said: "As this is a legal matter, which has been resolved, we will not be providing any further comment at this time."York became a co-owner of Rangers through 49ers Enterprises, the investment arm linked to the NFL's San Francisco 49ers, where he serves as chief executive and principal owner.In May 2025, a consortium led by US businessman Andrew Cavenagh and 49ers Enterprises completed a takeover of Rangers after acquiring a controlling 51% stake in the Scottish Premiership club.Cavenagh became Rangers chairman, with 49ers Enterprises taking a leading role in the club's ownership.The takeover followed months of negotiations and brought Rangers under majority American-backed ownership.49ers Enterprises first invested in Leeds United in 2018 when the club was in the Championship, steadily increasing its investment as the Whites returned to the Premier League following a 16-year absence, before assuming full control in 2023.As an NFL owner, York is subject to league policies. "We are aware of the matter which will be reviewed under the personal conduct policy," the NFL said.

schema.headline: Leeds and Rangers co-owner jailed after prostitution arrest

title: Sir Billy Boston: 'A world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told'
description: When Sir Billy Boston was knighted in 2025, it was a unique moment for rugby league.For the first time, this rebel sport from the north of England had
body: When Sir Billy Boston was knighted in 2025, it was a unique moment for rugby league.For the first time, this rebel sport from the north of England had been recognised in such a manner; one of its heroes had been acknowledged for their contribution to history through the game.Sir Billy was a fitting recipient of the honour and a world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told.You can tell the importance of someone by how many statutes have been erected in tribute, and Sir Billy Boston wasn't lacking.His name was chosen as one of just five to grace Wembley's monument to rugby league's Challenge Cup, while years after his departure north, his home city of Cardiff also ensured his legacy remained cast-iron strong as he formed part of a three-man tribute along with Clive Sullivan and Gus Risman.Unsurprisingly, Boston is also captured in bronze in his adopted home of Wigan; the place where his legend really came to life.Born and brought up in Cardiff's ethnically-eclectic Tiger Bay district, he learned his rugby skills on the streets and with the talent factory-esque Cardiff International Athletic Club. Like all Welsh lads he harboured dreams of playing for his local club Cardiff RFC and hopefully the national team.Like others before and after for a time, Boston found those routes blocked, having to travel to Neath and Pontypridd to trial before his military service took him north.It was here where the league scouts came calling, and Wigan persuaded Boston to turn professional in 1953, forever ending his union dreams in the time of 'sine die' penalties for liaising with league personnel.The money was life changing. £3,000 could easily buy a house at that stage, while it proved money well spent as he took to the new code like a duck to water, scoring with his first touch in a Wigan A team game.This prime specimen of Welsh breezeblock had everything; he was quick, he could step and as former player and BBC commentator Ray French put it - his fend was like "being hit in the face with shovel".The sepia footage and slow shutter speeds of the cameras that captured his magic during his playing days simply cannot dull his brilliance. Whether it was bustling over for another try in cherry and white hoops at Wembley or crushing the Aussies at Sydney Cricket Ground, Boston was a blur of speed, footwork and power.Having swiftly progressed to the first team at Central Park, he would go on to score 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan, and tales of his feats would be passed down through generations. There are very few down at the Brick Community Stadium these days who don't know of Sir Billy, young or old, his name carried a cache right until his last.Great Britain gave him the international recognition denied to him by Wales, and he rewarded the selectors by racking up the tries, particularly against the Australians who would bear the brunt of his scoring ability.He scored 36 tries alone on his maiden Great Britain tour, dazzling both Australia and New Zealand in 1954 under captain and fellow Welshman Dickie Williams.Boston was a phenomenal rugby league player, but there is also a powerful message in how in post-war Britain a black athlete could become a hugely popular figure by communities adjusting to a new, more diverse world.Others like Roy Francis beforehand, Johnny Freeman, and Colin Dixon, also became established names, but never quite sprinkled the same stardust as Sir Billy.It paved the way for players such as Ellery Hanley and Martin Offiah to charm the public with their talents, while modern day talent such as Junior Nsemba and Kai Pearce-Paul continues to stand out in a sport which has broken down barriers for years.Sir Billy had a unique unifying effect on a normally partisan and tribal rugby league community. He was revered naturally in Wigan, his adopted home, but you won't hear a boo or jeer at mention of Boston anywhere - not even at sworn rivals St Helens where they appreciate a good footballer when they see one.Still a regular visitor to Wigan games right up to his passing, it was always a beautiful moment when the cameras found him, the crowd spotting him on the screen bursting into cheer, and the realisation creeping over his face in the shape of a smile.There was a photo of him and his wife Lady Joan, who had died just a few weeks previously, on her seat with flowers at Wigan's game with Wakefield last week. There is a poignancy that Sir Billy departed soon after her.His seat will always be reserved at Wigan, and he will be dearly missed but certainly not forgotten.

schema.headline: Sir Billy Boston: 'A world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told'

title: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?
description: China is the biggest buyer of Iranian goods, making up 26.9% of its exports in 2025, according data from the International Trade Centre (ITC), a subsi
body: China is the biggest buyer of Iranian goods, making up 26.9% of its exports in 2025, according data from the International Trade Centre (ITC), a subsidiary of the United Nations and the World Trade Organisation.There a few caveats to ITC's data, which covers a period before the US-Israel war with Iran began.First, several economists believe that even before the conflict started, a lot of Iranian oil sales, particularly to China, were underreported for political reasons.Second, the ITC tallies Iran's exports using mostly the import numbers reported by its trading partners - owing to the difficulty in getting up to date export data from Iran.Third, import data for some of Iran's trading partners, such as Iraq, is incomplete.Despite this, Iranian trade's importance to China is clear from its response to the US announcement of "economic D-Day".It said that it was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions", that economic pressure tactics would not help resolve problems and that Beijing would safeguard its own interests.Like Turkey, Pakistan borders Iran and is one of its biggest export partners, according to ITC data, while also being keen to maintain a good relationship with the US.But unlike Turkey, Pakistan's top export partner is instead the US, meaning it has more to lose from any economic punishment imposed by Washington.It is also a key mediator in peace talks between the US and Iran, meaning a breakdown in its relationship with either country could make finding a solution to the conflict even more challenging.The other complicating factor is that not all of Pakistan's trade with Iran is within the Pakistan government's control.The BBC has seen evidence that oil is being smuggled across the border from Iran to Pakistan en masse by bikers, some as young as 15.This was the case before the Iran war began, but data suggests the practice has picked up since.And though the US and Pakistan's oil firms have pressured Pakistan's government to clamp down on the practice, it has struggled to police remote parts of the 900km border.The BBC has previously asked the Iranian government to comment on the allegation that it is involved in the fuel smuggling. It did not respond.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the sanctions against Iran will "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue".Yet, many experts disagree. Advisory firm Oxford Economics said the direct impact on Iran's revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".Ali Vaez, deputy director at the International Crisis Group, said: "Anything that moves in Iran has already been sanctioned by multiple layers of sanctions, in fact. "So the question now is one of enforcement. Does the United States have what it takes to impose fines and levies on countries that continue to trade with Iran?"He noted how the US started an economic war with China, Iran's biggest trading partner, last year but "backed out of it".Former senior advisor at the state department Aya Ibrahim said the US's overreliance on them "incentivises countries to find ways around that system".She also raised concerns that the sanctions may have the biggest affect on people, rather than economies, as they "deny people necessities to stay alive".Meanwhile, global markets have had a muted response to the announcement.Global oil prices fell following the announcement, but are still far higher than pre-war levels. Stock traders were even less moved by the news, with the major indexes of the biggest companies listed in the US, Europe, and Asia barely shifting.The US will has a way to go before it convinces economists, investors, and the nations trading with Iran that its sanctions threat is to be taken seriously.Additional reporting by Miguel Roca-Terry

schema.headline: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?

title: Goodbye Savinho, hello Savio: Tottenham sign winger from Man City for £75m
description: Savio's move to north London has been more than 12 months in the making, with Spurs failing in a bid to sign him last summer when Thomas Frank was in
body: Savio's move to north London has been more than 12 months in the making, with Spurs failing in a bid to sign him last summer when Thomas Frank was in charge.He opted to remain at Etihad Stadium, but his game time was limited under former City boss Pep Guardiola last term, making just seven Premier League starts."It's taken a while but I'm very happy to be here," said Savio, who has 13 caps for his country but was not part of their World Cup squad."It's a wonderful opportunity at a brilliant club with one of the best managers in the world."As soon as I spoke to the head coach I knew I had to come. He told me he wants to help me reach the highest level, and I believe we can do that together, as a team."Savio joined City from French side Troyes in a £30.8m deal two years ago and made 84 appearances, scoring seven goals and providing 16 assists.His arrival at Spurs follows those of Mateus Fernandes from West Ham, Sandro Tonali from Newcastle and Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton this summer, with spending reaching a combined £312m.Spurs have also brought in defenders Marcos Senesi and Andy Robertson, and goalkeeper Martin Dubravka, on free transfers."Savio is a player who brings energy, imagination and quality in wide positions. He has the courage to attack defenders and the ability to change a game with his creativity," added De Zerbi.Spurs are also in advanced talks to buy Egypt forward Omar Marmoush from City, and sources with knowledge of the situation say there is a "good chance" the deal gets completed before the 1 September transfer deadline.Savio's involvement for City fell sharply last season after the club signed winger Antoine Semenyo from Bournemouth in January.He played 821 Premier League minutes, scoring once and providing one assist, while featuring in only 31% of City's available minutes across all competitions.That was a significant drop from the previous campaign, when he played 54% of City's minutes.Yet his 2024-25 numbers show why Tottenham are prepared to invest heavily in him. Savio registered eight Premier League assists that season, all from open play, despite playing only 1,773 minutes. Only five players recorded more from open play.On a per-90 basis, he ranked third for open-play assists with 0.41, while only Mohamed Salah created more chances per 90 than Savio's 2.2.His biggest threat, though, came from carrying the ball. Among Premier League players with at least 1,000 minutes in 2024-25, only Jeremy Doku averaged more progressive carries of at least 10 metres than Savio's 6.8 per 90 minutes.Savio also led the division for carries followed by a chance created, averaging 1.3 per 90, while only Son Heung-min ended a carry with an assist more frequently.  Savio also completed 2.6 dribbles per 90 with a 51% success rate and used those carries to draw defenders towards him before releasing team-mates.That ability was even more evident during his breakout 2023-24 season on loan at Girona. Savio played 2,989 minutes in La Liga in 2023-24, with 65% of them coming on the left wing. He scored nine goals, supplied eight assists and established himself as one of the division's most dangerous one-against-one players.At City his role shifted. Across his two Premier League seasons, his most common position was on the right, accounting for 36% of his minutes, compared with 20% on the left. That versatility could matter at Spurs.

schema.headline: Goodbye Savinho, hello Savio: Tottenham sign winger from Man City for £75m

title: Father's house was rammed by car before son died in A66 crash
description: A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.Cole Worthy, 17, was
body: A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

schema.headline: Father's house was rammed by car before son died in A66 crash

title: Carlos Baleba: Manchester United sign Cameroon midfielder from Brighton in £70m deal
description: Manchester United have signed Cameroon midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton in a £70m deal.The Old Trafford club have paid an initial £65m, plus a p
body: Manchester United have signed Cameroon midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton in a £70m deal.The Old Trafford club have paid an initial £65m, plus a potential £5m in add-ons, for the 22-year-old, while Brighton have negotiated a sell-on clause.United targeted Baleba after deciding to strengthen their midfield further following the summer arrivals of Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa.Baleba has signed a five year-contract at Old Trafford, with the option to extend for a further year."It is an incredible feeling to join the club of my dreams," he said. "Playing at Old Trafford is always special, but the opportunity to do so as a Manchester United player will be a real honour."I cannot wait to work with Michael Carrick. His experience and knowledge of the game make him the perfect coach to help me to reach the highest level."The ambition of everyone at the club is extremely clear, the future is hugely exciting, and I am determined to play my part in delivering the success that we are capable of together."Baleba's move follows United's shock 2-0 defeat by Hull City in Saturday's Premier League opener, where Santos and Tielemans made their midfield debuts.United reignited their interest after attempting to sign him last year near deadline day, but were put off by Brighton's valuation, which was in excess of £100m.Baleba, who joined Brighton from Lille in 2023, is currently sidelined with an ankle injury he picked up during the Seagulls' pre-season training camp in Austria.He made 112 appearances for Brighton, scoring four times, and 31 in the Premier League last season as they finished eighth to qualify for this season's Conference League.The move has taken United's summer spending up to £153m as they prepare for a return to the Champions League for the first time since the 2023-24 campaign.United will hope for the 2024-25 version of Baleba rather than last season's because it was his performances in that campaign that attracted them.We can't know what would have happened if the approach for Mateus Fernandes had been successful, nor if Mason Mount had not suffered the injury in the pre-season game with Paris St-Germain two weeks ago that ruled him out of the Premier League opener.However, even before Saturday's disappointing loss at Hull it is clear that, despite adding Santos and Tielemans to their midfield ranks, they still lack physicality and power.In theory, Baleba should solve that issue.The 22-year-old is strong in possession, covers ground quickly, is good in the air and alert to danger.Crucially, he also has three years' worth of top-flight experience in England behind him, having moved to Brighton from Lille when he was 19. It gives him the edge on Santos, also 22, and it will be interesting to see whether the pair compete for the same place at the base of Michael Carrick's midfield or if, against the best sides, they might play together.It will also be fascinating to see if he gets asked to fill in at left-back too.He has played there before and, unlike Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui - who could also switch sides if Luke Shaw is unavailable - is left-footed.Paul Pogba is the only midfield player United have signed for more than the £70m they are committing to Baleba which, given his age, is a statement in itself.Baleba's appeal lies less in creativity and more in his ability to win possession, cover ground and then carry his team forward.His 2025-26 campaign was quieter than the previous one, but his 2024-25 numbers show why United have tracked him for so long. He ranked fourth among Premier League midfielders for possessions won in the middle third (107) and interceptions (46), was fifth for ball recoveries (197) and seventh for duels won (199).That defensive output was matched by his ability to progress possession himself. Baleba averaged 6.7 progressive carries per 90 minutes, with only three qualifying Premier League defensive midfielders recording more, while 2.9 of those carries travelled at least 10 metres.His athleticism underpins that game as he reached a top speed of 34.5km/h in 2024-25, compared with 30.5km/h for Casemiro, and averaged 8.2 defensive actions per 90.He is not necessarily the midfielder United would rely on to dictate possession. Only 11.8% of his passes were classed as line-breaking that season and 22.7% travelled forward - both below the average for central and defensive midfielders.But that may make him complementary to United's other options rather than a direct alternative. Tielemans can provide more of the progressive distribution, while Baleba offers defensive security and the ability to drive through midfield. Alongside Kobbie Mainoo, he could take on more of the ball-winning and ground-covering work, while a partnership with Santos could allow Baleba greater freedom to operate box to box.That versatility is reflected in his positioning as he spent 88% of his minutes last season as a defensive midfielder and 12% in central midfield, suggesting he can anchor the side or step forward depending on who plays alongside him.United most commonly defended in a 4-2-2-2 last season under Carrick, accounting for 55.9% of their out-of-possession shapes. Baleba's dynamism could be especially valuable in a system where central midfielders are asked to defend large spaces and stop counter-attacks.There may, however, be an adaptation period. Baleba is recovering from an ankle ligament injury suffered in pre-season and will need time to recover his match sharpness.United have also looked to spend longer spells in possession under Carrick, progressing through midfield with quick combinations. Baleba's game is better suited to more open contests, but his passing profile suggests he may need time to adjust to greater responsibility in build-up.His left foot and mobility should still make him a natural partner for players such as Tielemans or Bruno Fernandes. There is development ahead of him at 22, not least after last season's dip, but at his best Baleba combines defensive activity with the acceleration and carrying power to transform a turnover into an attack within seconds.

schema.headline: Carlos Baleba: Manchester United sign Cameroon midfielder from Brighton in £70m deal

title: Billy Boston: Legendary Wigan, Wales and GB winger dies aged 92
description: Boston would go on to score 24 tries in 31 appearances for Great Britain and was part of the side that won the 1960 World Cup, scoring a try in the fi
body: Boston would go on to score 24 tries in 31 appearances for Great Britain and was part of the side that won the 1960 World Cup, scoring a try in the final as they beat Australia 10-3 at Odsal Stadium in Bradford.Boston finished his playing career as a second row with Blackpool Borough.In all, Boston scored 571 tries in his career - a total surpassed only by Australian legend Brian Bevan in top-class rugby league -  and is one of the truly great British rugby league players.After his retirement from the game, Boston ran the Griffin Hotel close to Wigan's Central Park Ground where one of the stands was named after the Welshman.Boston was among the first players inducted into the Rugby League Hall of Fame in 1988 and is one of five rugby league players to be included in a statue at Wembley Stadium.He is immortalised in two more statues, in Wigan where he is an adopted son and in his home city of Cardiff.Boston was appointed an MBE in 1986, and was among the first to be inducted into the Welsh Sports Hall of Fame, external when it was launched in 1990.In 2025, and having being diagnosed with dementia, he was awarded the highest honour, a knighthood by King Charles.His death comes just weeks after the passing of his wife, Lady Joan.Tributes have been led by prime minister Andy Burnham who said he was a "giant of a man in every way"."Heartbroken to hear my friend Sir Billy Boston has died," he said on social media."Billy was one of the greatest rugby league players of all time but also one of the kindest and most down-to-earth people you could ever wish to meet."He always had time for people and gave so much to back to his adopted home, Wigan."I will miss him greatly and am thinking today of Billy's family, still grieving the recent loss of his beloved wife Joan."Wigan owner Mike Danson said: "Billy Boston was everybody's hero, including my mum's."His achievements in rugby league were extraordinary, and his knighthood was a fitting recognition of a career that brought great credit to Wigan and to the game."But Billy's legacy was not simply what he achieved. It was the humility with which he carried it. Despite everything he accomplished, he remained a quiet, dignified and deeply respected man."He leaves behind an example that will endure for generations. Our thoughts are with his family and those closest to him."A great man, and a true Wigan legend. He will be remembered with pride and affection."In a statement, Wales Rugby League said: "Today, rugby league has lost one of its greatest-ever players, Wales has lost one of its finest sporting sons, and our sport has lost a truly special gentleman."The WRU also paid tribute, calling Boston "one of the best loved and most iconic figures in the history of Welsh sport".Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy added: "He was, in my view, the greatest rugby league player of all time and one of the nicest people I've ever had the privilege to know."Matt Newsum, BBC rugby league commentatorIt is testament to the star power of Sir Billy Boston that even 56 years after he last graced a rugby pitch, young fans are fully aware of the legend that is the Welshman from Cardiff's Tiger Bay.He had a uniquely unifying effect on a normally partisan and tribal rugby league community. Revered naturally in Wigan, his adopted home, but you won't hear a boo or jeer at mention of Boston anywhere - not even at sworn rivals St Helens where they appreciate a good footballer when they see one.The sepia footage and slow shutter-speeds of the cameras that captured the magic of his playing days simply cannot dull his brilliance; whether it's bustling over for another try in cherry and white hoops at Wembley or crushing the Aussies at the Sydney Cricket Ground, Boston is a blur of speed, footwork and power.Wing or centre, a wonderful finisher and a player whose innate talents were honed on those tough streets of his district - one that also produced fellow pioneers Roy Francis and Colin Dixon.Many a fan will have drunk at the pub which provided some of his post-playing focus, the Griffin Hotel, close to the Central Park ground he scored so many of his 571 tries on - the best strike rate of any British player.Still a regular visitor to Wigan games right up to his death, it was always a beautiful moment when the cameras found him, the crowd spotting him on the screen bursting into cheer, and the realisation creeping over his face in the shape of a smile.It will take some getting used to, the empty seat at the Brick. He will be missed but certainly not forgotten.

schema.headline: Billy Boston: Legendary Wigan, Wales and GB winger dies aged 92

title: Food influencers v critics: Why credibility counts
description: Image source, Oscar BostockImage caption, "Creators certainly have an influence on how people go out to eat, for sure," says Bristol influencer Oscar
body: Image source, Oscar BostockImage caption, "Creators certainly have an influence on how people go out to eat, for sure," says Bristol influencer Oscar BostockByJasmine Ketibuah-FoleyWest of EnglandWhen stuck for ideas about where to eat on a Friday night or torn between takeaways, more and more people are turning to social media and their favourite content creators for inspiration.Research by one Bristol food writer has raised questions about transparency, with some creators guaranteeing positive coverage in advance and offering not to make clear their review was in exchange for a free meal.Those promises of good reviews were made before they had eaten a bite - or realised the restaurant they had been asked to promote did not exist.So can diners trust influencers to give an honest opinion and what is their role in shaping where we eat? We asked people in the food scene to share their thoughts.Meg Houghton-Gilmour, food writer and founder of The Bristol Sauce, undertook a two-part research piece, external into the world of food influencing when she created a website and social media account for a fake Japanese restaurant "coming soon to Bristol". She messaged 48 influencers asking how much they would charge to make content, what would guarantee positive coverage and whether they would declare it an advert.After receiving 33 responses, she said the prices quoted by influencers varied widely. Some said they would post in exchange for free food and drink, without an extra payment on top - and five of those said they would post without labelling the content as an advert.UK advertising rules state paid posts must be clearly marked with #ad or a platform's paid partnership feature. This includes free meals in exchange for posts.Houghton-Gilmour added the requests she sent out had created a swell of "misleading" positive noise on social media around the upcoming opening."I realised how insular and repetitive it is. Everyone going to the same places, saying the same thing," she said.Image source, Meg Houghton-GilmourImage caption, Meg Houghton-Gilmour said her research offered "a fascinating insight" into the world of influencersWith more than 135,000 followers on Instagram, external and millions of views on TikTok, external, Oscar Bostock, also known as Bos Finesse, is a driving force as a food creator in Bristol and said becoming an influencer was a "no-brainer"."There are food creators in the social media space, like myself, who do have a lot of credibility. But we need to respect the culture a bit as well."You'll never beat the people that write about food for a living. I don't really like to review and criticise food - I'll leave that to the professionals. "At the same time, you need people here like myself to just celebrate food," he adds.Bostock says authenticity is very important to him, and told the BBC there are many places he has said no to reviewing or reflecting. "It's worth explaining it, being paid for a restaurant to say, 'this is good' is completely different to being  paid to promote a new menu or venue. "I feel very strongly about it, anywhere I work with had to be a place I actually valued and would visit in my own time."Image source, Jay RaynerImage caption, Consumers needed to know whether someone had paid for the meal they were talking about, said food critic Jay RaynerFood critic Jay Rayner, who writes for the Financial Times, believes his role is to write "as interesting, entertaining [and] truthful column" as he can."I don't think there's much truth in the idea that the newspaper critic is dead," he said. "What I see happening is an awful lot more media around restaurants, full stop."I know, anecdotally, that a good review from me still results in many bookings, which is lovely - but it's not actually a concern of mine."He said people sometimes ask if influencers "pose a challenge to what you do"."My response is, 'only if it's better than what I do'," said Rayner, stressing his authority as a critic is not unassailable. "I do not have a right to my lofty perch."Rayner said newspapers such as the Financial Times would "pick up the bill" for critics writing reviews, whereas a lot of influencers were invited to eat for nothing, which is something consumers should be aware of."That does undermine the credibility of the review," he said. "[But] you know, we're all celebrating the culture of eating food and eating out."Image source, Adam ArmstrongImage caption, Chef Adam Armstrong said influencers, like critics, offer an opinion which "you don't have to look at"Adam Armstrong, head chef at Bath's Emberwood, said the sort of promotion restaurants received from influencers was something the industry would have been "screaming out for" years ago."If you make a bit of noise here or there, it just puts you on the map," he said.He acknowledged many people had a "negative" view of food creators, but added: "People give them too much reverence in the first place. They're just people with an opinion."The Nook Cheltenham, in Gloucestershire, has worked hard at being Instagram-friendly, currently boasting more than 11,000 followers.Director and founder Edward Surman said: "Social media is a place where brands can alter their own story - where it's not moved around by the press."Surman maintains influencers are not replacing food critics, but more of an "augmentation". Image source, Baljinder Kaur Sangha-GillImage caption, Baljinder Kaur Gill said influencers had opened up the conversation about foodWiltshire-based food influencer Baljinder Kaur Sangha-Gill, also known as The Authentic Punjabee, says her pages have moved beyond a list of recommendations and have come to represent a community of friends."Influencers haven't replaced critics. We've just opened the conversation about food," she said."Years ago, when you were looking for a restaurant or recipe, you'd wait for the Sunday paper. Now you can just go onto TikTok."But she cautions not everything on social media is reliable."People will get free things to promote something. You've got to be aware of that. I'm very careful with that, I don't lie to my followers," she added.Following her research, Houghton-Gilmour added: "Influencers are a symptom of the society and tech world we live in - not the problem. It's the tech billionaires making it unclear what's an ad and what's not."She said the problem was not people making content but the lack of transparency, although she accepted that was not true of all influencers.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Bristol

schema.headline: Food influencers v critics: Why credibility counts

title: Brydon Carse: Joe Root says he is 'hacked off' and 'disappointed' at nightclub incident
description: England captain Joe Root says he is "hacked off" and "disappointed" at the incident involving fast bowler Brydon Carse at a Derby nightclub.Carse, 31,
body: England captain Joe Root says he is "hacked off" and "disappointed" at the incident involving fast bowler Brydon Carse at a Derby nightclub.Carse, 31, was dropped from the squad for the second Test starting against Pakistan this week. Images that appeared on social media on Sunday showed Carse in handcuffs outside a bar in Derby on Saturday night and he was briefly arrested and subsequently de-arrested."If I'm being brutally honest, I'm really hacked off, I'm really disappointed," Root said in the opening to a news conference."After last week's performance, we're sat here and we're talking about something that is not related to it at all."The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has referred the incident to the Cricket Regulator and Carse was replaced in the squad by Sonny Baker, with the Test starting at Lord's on Thursday.Carse was not on England duty at the time of the incident as he was released to play for Durham, but he is a centrally contracted player. Root also said he had spoken to his England team-mate about the incident, and expressed his frustration at the "stupid mistakes" that are continually being made."I've spoken to Brydon, and when I first found out my main concern was him as a person," Root added."I don't think I'm speaking out of turn by saying he's very upset, very apologetic and understands his actions. I'm sure that when he gets his chance he will say that himself. "But I don't think it's the isolated incident itself, it's the fact we keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it's detracting from what we're doing on the field."In October, England white-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer outside a nightclub in Wellington, New Zealand, with team-mates Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue also present.During the Ashes tour of Australia, opener Ben Duckett was filmed apparently drunk on England's holiday in Noosa.And in June, former Test captain Ben Stokes and pace bowler Gus Atkinson broke a team curfew and were present when a member of England's security staff was punched by a Saracens rugby player in a London nightclub.In this latest incident, Carse was with Durham team-mates Stokes and Matthew Potts, all of whom are under England central contracts. In Stokes' case, the England deal remains in place despite his international retirement in June.It makes a total of eight contracted players who have been involved in or present for late-night incidents in the past year – more than a quarter of the 30 men on England deals.When he was reappointed as Test captain, Root confirmed he would remove the midnight curfew which was previously in place during Stokes and Brendon McCullum's regime after a string of off-field incidents during the Ashes over the winter.Root stood by that decision, saying he still did not think it was "the right way to go", but admitted it would take some time for the team to be trusted by the fans again. "In many ways we're going to have to earn a lot of trust back, and it's something that we're going to have to live and breathe consistently," he said."I might only be in this dressing room for a couple more years, but there is a group of players there who might be in there for another 10. "We've had a very strong discussion about what's expected of everyone when they play for England, what the standards are that we have to uphold, not just on the field but off it."I've made it very clear how we want to conduct ourselves, and now we've got to live it and show people what I see day in, day out in the dressing room, which is a group of characters who know what it means to play for England and not having incidents define how we are seen as players. That's going to take some work and time."Root also confirmed he had spoken to his predecessor Stokes, who was also seen in the social media video, but only to check in on Carse's wellbeing.He was asked what potential consequences Carse might face but said he would have no involvement as it is in the hands of the regulator, and was keen to reiterate that he was focusing on moving forward and "building something to be proud of"."I don't think the recent past has been a good look," Root, 35, said."It's our responsibility to change that. I see the dressing room every day and how we operate around cricket and it's very impressive. "But at the same time, I can understand why we are viewed in a certain way and in a certain light at the moment. "That's what lies ahead of us, to change that. I just think, if we don't put ourselves in certain situations, it's not something we will have to worry about."If there was any question as to why England turned to Joe Root for a second stint as Test captain, if he is the right man for the job, then this address at Lord's removed all of those doubts.Root showed himself to be the leader England need in this moment. Clearly ticking over what happened at the weekend, Root was able to strike the balance between letting his feelings be known, showing compassion for Brydon Carse and not pre-judging the investigation that is ongoing.There have been plenty of these kinds of news conferences over the past year: someone wearing an England badge explaining a misdemeanour, promising to do better. This time, when Root spoke, his words were plausible and believable.Some wondered why Root was the one left to face the media, rather than members of the management team like director of cricket Rob Key or chief executive Richard Gould.Maybe it is because no-one else was able to speak with Root's gravitas. No-one in a suit, not Ben Stokes, nor Harry Brook. Perhaps this is the most impressive display of leadership anyone connected with English cricket has shown for some time.It should leave no one – especially not the England players – in any doubt where their captain stands on this issue. For any athlete to tell the world they are "hacked off" with a team-mate is a stark message.Root addressed his England team on Tuesday morning. If the captain was able to speak like this in public, one can only wonder about the sternness of the message delivered in private. Carse would not have been there, but plenty of others who have erred in the past year would have been in the room.There will be no return for the midnight curfew, but Root was also quite clear about players avoiding situations that could lead to trouble. "Stupid mistakes", he called them. He hammered home the point that players will not find trouble if they do not put themselves in the places where trouble could find them.But Root also regularly mentioned the notion of this team now having an opportunity to build something on and off the field. Put simply, their reputation in the eyes of the public cannot get much lower, so the only direction is improvement.Amid all the controversy, English cricket is fortunate to have Root. Not only is he a bona fide all-time great, but also a superb example of how all sportspeople should go about their business on and off the field.Last week, before his first Test back in charge, Root asked his players to be "good role models and good human beings". They should look no further than their captain for inspiration.

schema.headline: Brydon Carse: Joe Root says he is 'hacked off' and 'disappointed' at nightclub incident

title: Man Utd transfer news: Will Michael Carrick's side buy a left-back before transfer window closes?
description: Man Utd's midfield spending is done - now for a left-back?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester United full-back Luke Shaw started all 3
body: Man Utd's midfield spending is done - now for a left-back?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester United full-back Luke Shaw started all 38 Premier League games in the 2025-26 seasonByManchester United reporterThe signing of Carlos Baleba completes a £155m summer revamp of Manchester United's midfield.At the end of last season, midfield was targeted as a priority area as United looked to build on qualification for the Champions League after a two-year absence.Baleba arrives along with Andrey Santos, a £48m signing from Chelsea, and £35m former Aston Villa man Youri Tielemans.It means that, along with England's Kobbie Mainoo, United now have a spread of different attributes across their four-man midfield, three of whom are 22 or younger.But, at Manchester United, one bad result brings intense pressure.Even Michael Carrick's calm exterior cracked in a post-match exchange with former Middlesbrough and Swindon Town forward Jan Aage Fjortoft, now a TV presenter for Viaplay, following the shock defeat at Hull when the Norwegian suggested there was a lack of passion in United's ranks."Come on, that's ridiculous," replied Carrick. "You played football. You understand. That's a ridiculous thing to say."So, now the midfield is sorted, it is natural for fans to look at the other areas of Carrick's squad that could do with reinforcements; namely left-back.Figure caption, Highlights: Hull shock Man United on opening weekendHow many games can Shaw play?Signing an additional left-back has looked an obvious thing for Manchester United to do.Luke Shaw started all 38 Premier League games last season. He started at Hull. Of United's past 44 league games, the 31-year-old England international has failed to start just one, the final game of the 2024-25 campaign, four days after the Europa League final defeat by Tottenham – and he went on the post-season tour of Asia immediately afterwards.But, before that, Shaw's injury record had not been great.Between February 2024 and April 2025, he played as many games for England (three) as he did for his club. He missed three months at the start of the 2023-24 campaign.There were calf and hamstring issues but also a feeling Erik ten Hag rushed him back too quickly.More than anyone, Shaw benefited from a 40-game season, allowing him to prepare properly, largely for one game a week, sometimes not even that.That preparation time will not be repeated.Although there are blank midweeks between Manchester United's first three games, if they get through two EFL Cup rounds, they will not have a full midweek without a game, other than during international breaks, until the one that includes Christmas Day.It is the combination of Shaw's injury record and the crush of games that has led to the feeling another left-back will arrive.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester United are keen on Newcastle's England defender Lewis HallThere is no doubt the club like Newcastle's Lewis Hall. At 21, he is the right age profile and ideally suited to challenging Shaw for his place, with the safety net of there being enough games to keep both men happy.However, Newcastle don't want to sell. It would take a huge offer to persuade them otherwise and Manchester United's powerbrokers have proved on numerous occasions this summer they will not be held to ransom, or overpay, for players.In addition, how much money do they have to spend?In published third-quarter financial accounts to 31 March, United confirmed they owed £405.75m in outstanding transfer fees, £171.14m of which was due after more than one year. The club are still to outline what the additional $125m (£91.64m) they borrowed in a wider refinancing announced in June will be used for.The assumption is £70m for Baleba, equal the sum United paid for Casemiro in 2022 and a figure only exceeded in their history in terms of midfielders by the club record £89m spent on Paul Pogba, is at the top end of what they wanted to pay.Plenty of alternative left-backs to Hall have been mentioned.Racing Santander's 19-year-old Jorge Salinas has a €16m (£13.7m) release clause, but is also coveted by Atletico Madrid.Barcelona's Alejandro Balde was left out of the 5-0 La Liga victory over Elche by coach Hansi Flick, to allow him to "clear his mind" amid intense transfer speculation, with United among those to be linked with the 22-year-old Spain international. Barcelona are said to value him between €30m (£25.66m) and €40m (£34.22m).Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Joshua Zirkzee was an unused substitute in Manchester United's defeat at HullWith a week to go before the transfer window closes, the situation is thought to be fluid, but caution in United circles around the expectations of a new left-back being signed is being stressed.A significant sale could change the dynamic.However, the idea of Marcus Rashford leaving has virtually been ruled out with confirmation he will wear the coveted number nine shirt this season, while the anticipated exit of Manuel Ugarte had to be scrapped when he was injured at the World Cup.Of Carrick's senior squad, forward Joshua Zirkzee appears surplus to requirements, yet with fitness doubts over Amad Diallo – the club are choosing to offer no clarification on the extent of his injury amid a report he could be out for up to six weeks – it is uncertain whether interest from Serie A will lead to a sale.Carrick does have options at left-back without bringing anyone else in. Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have both switched flanks in the past, while Baleba, a left-footed player, has played at full-back for Brighton previously.In addition, Harry Amass was Shaw's back-up during pre-season and the 19-year-old remains at United. But he was not included in Carrick's squad for the Hull trip and the expectation has been he will leave, either permanently or on loan.Most still think there will be another left-back in Carrick's squad when the transfer window closes on 1 September – but it is by no means certain.Figure caption, 'They just didn't look fit at all' - Shearer on Man UtdFollow Manchester United on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical United contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about the Red Devils

title: China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners
description: China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include
body: China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing.Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports.Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."Bessent described the plans for sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country.He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions".The US has dubbed its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran.It comes almost six months after the start of the Iran war.The conflict has since led to hikes in oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz - a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed traffic via its own naval blockade.Recent attempts to end the conflict via diplomacy have failed, and a 60-day ceasefire formally expired last week with no sign of a settlement.With the announcement of new sanctions, the US treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".Iran is already under heavy sanctions from the US, but Bessent said these go further.He said the Treasury had mapped financial channels, facilitators and networks used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil, imposing sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.But analysts had cast doubt on the latest measures even before China's response. David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the BBC the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib". "We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added.This is partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions. They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate."And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass it onto the people.Other trade partners that could be affected by the US announcement include India and Russia, who have not yet responded.

schema.headline: China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners

title: OnlyFans owner was paid over $700m before his death
description: The late owner of streaming platform OnlyFans was paid more than $700m (£513m) in dividends before his death from cancer earlier this year.Fenix Inter
body: The late owner of streaming platform OnlyFans was paid more than $700m (£513m) in dividends before his death from cancer earlier this year.Fenix International Ltd, the British company that owns OnlyFans, made $714m in profit before tax last year, it said in its annual report. This is an increase of 5% from 2024.The site hosts a range of subscription-based content from cooking to fitness videos, but it is best known for pornography and is credited with transforming online adult content by encouraging personal connection between sex workers and subscribers.Its owner Leonid Radvinsky, who died earlier this year aged 43, bought the site from its British founders in 2018.OnlyFans employs just 47 people. Companies with such high profits rarely have such small staff - for example, British retail giant Marks and Spencer, which employs over 65,000 people, made £671m in profit last year.Fenix International's company results show that it paid dividends of $535m for the year ending 30 November 2025, with further dividends payments totalling $174m between then and 26 March 2026. Radvinsky, who was born in Ukraine and raised in the US, died on 23 March. The company is now owned by his widow, Yekaterina 'Katie' Chudnovsky.OnlyFans surged in popularity during the Covid-19 pandemic, landing Radvinsky on Forbes' annual list of billionaires just three years later.The site is known for the way it encourages creators and fans to connect through livestreams, personalised messages, and direct requests for custom-made photos and videos.In return for hosting the material, OnlyFans takes a 20% share of all payments.The site had 132 million paying subscribers and 2.5 million active creators in 2025. The boom in size and popularity under Radvinsky's ownership also brought scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators over its adult content — a recent BBC Three documentary uncovered allegations of exploitation, coercion and violence committed against OnlyFans creators.In 2024, British regulators launched an investigation into whether children were accessing porn, an issue that the company at the time blamed on a technical issue.Ofcom ultimately dropped that probe, but it fined the firm about £1m, external for failing to respond accurately to its requests for information about the measures it had in place to check the age of its users, who in theory must be 18 or over.Creators have also debunked the narrative that making explicit videos on the site is a get-rich-quick scheme.Keily Blair, the chief executive of OnlyFans, said on Tuesday that the company had paid over $30bn to creators since launching a decade ago."OnlyFans provides real opportunities to real people by creating a safe, regulated space where people can monetise their content with a global fan base," she said."As a UK-based business we have also made a significant contribution to the UK economy, paying over £600 million in corporate taxes from 2016 to date."

schema.headline: OnlyFans owner was paid over $700m before his death

title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
description: Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows. Often left alone
body: Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows. Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.  On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed. Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in."I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.The report calls for better ways to prepare young people for adulthood and an overhaul of the workforce supporting them.The main source of support provided to young people who have left care comes through the framework of having a personal adviser (PA). The review found that the support provided by PAs can "vary greatly from place to place" with a "huge variation" in quality of practice.With minimum visiting requirements of once every two months, the authors say it is "not surprising" that some PAs they spoke to "hardly knew" the young person they were supporting.The report is also critical of the housing and accommodation support given to young adults, saying it is often from a "profit-making arm of the service with no specific requirements for a therapeutic or social work discipline", which needs to be redressed.The government says it is driving forward a national rollout of connected housing options for those leaving care, starting with £25 million this year. It says this will "significantly increase" young people's chances of being offered a "home that provides them with community and connection rather than leaving them isolated in inappropriate accommodation".Children's Minister Josh MacAlister said "enduring relationships" must become the "central obsession" of the care system. "Care must build and not break the relationships that young people need, and this must be the new North Star," he added.Izy Winter was put into care at 13. Now 25, she says she was let down at every stage."While I was in care I was cold, hungry and neglected," she says.As a care leaver she experienced failures that left her feeling "invisible and unprotected".Izy was living with an abusive partner, but welfare checks that should have picked up on this were not carried out correctly, she says."The person who was meant to check asked to meet me in the car park and got me to sign a piece of paper to say he'd been inside my home when he hadn't," she said.Izy has ADHD and dyslexia and struggles with paperwork. Her support worker did not check that she was receiving all the financial support she was entitled to. By the time she was made aware, it was too late and she could not reclaim the money she had missed out on."I was really struggling financially and was so frustrated that even when I asked for help, I wasn't given it."She says she is saddened, but not surprised, to read the new report."The recent findings reflect a reality that too many of us have lived through".If you've been affected by the issues in this story, you can find information, advice and support from the BBC's Action Line. Anyone feeling emotionally distressed or suicidal can call Samaritans for free on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org in the UK.

schema.headline: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'

title: Trump hopes sanctions will topple Iran's regime - its leaders are betting otherwise
description: The US says it has launched an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said sanct
body: The US says it has launched an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said sanctions included digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. Any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.However, Bessent's announcement of what he termed an "economic D-Day" may have sounded more dramatic in Washington than in Tehran.Shortly after the announcement, Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh called it "the same old talk" and said Iran was ready for "every scenario". He said Tehran had expected the measures and had plans to deal with them.His reaction points to the main question Iranian leaders are likely to be asking: What can the US do now that it has not already tried?Bessent has threatened wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran. But the basic policy is not new. Iran has faced US sanctions for years, including penalties against foreign companies trading with it.What matters to Tehran is whether Washington can enforce sanctions more widely than before.The US blockade has already made a difference. It has reduced Iran's ability to export as much oil by sea as it did before and made it harder to import goods and equipment. Iran has long land borders with seven countries and years of experience using them to bypass sanctions. But land routes cannot easily replace trade by sea, especially oil exports.The pressure could therefore become much more serious if Washington manages to close channels that survived previous sanctions, particularly those involving China and Iran's neighbours. That is a big ask. China's foreign ministry said on Tuesday that it firmly opposed the sanctions, calling them illegal.If the sanctions fail, Bessent's announcement could strengthen those inside Iran who oppose a deal with the US.They could argue that Washington has returned to economic pressure because its other choices are limited. A new military campaign carries risks, while years of sanctions have failed to force Iran to accept US demands.Washington has also left little room for diplomacy. Although Pakistan and other mediators are still trying to revive talks, the US has not ruled out further strikes. The renewed threats could weaken Iranian officials who favour a deal.It was already in deep trouble before the war, with high inflation and a rapidly weakening currency, and has deteriorated further since the fighting began with US and Israeli air strikes on 28 February. The weakening of the Iranian currency, the  rial, is felt sharply and widely. Imports cost more, businesses struggle to plan, and people's savings lose value. Restrictions on oil exports also reduce the government's access to foreign currency. Negin - not her real name - is a 34-year-old woman who says her monthly income is now about  $100 (£73). She told the BBC: "I don't go to the cinema, theatre, or concerts. I don't buy gifts for anyone. I don't attend birthday parties. I can only buy meat with the government subsidy voucher; otherwise, I wouldn't be able to afford it."Mona, a housewife with two kids, says her husband has been out of work since the beginning of the war. She adds: "We feel scared, especially after the sanctions that began yesterday. Ever since the war, my spouse has not gone back to work. He used to work on ships."She adds: "We're trying to manage our expenses as best we can, but we've definitely had to cut back on all of our extra spending and small luxuries."Iran may believe time is working against US President Donald Trump. Further disruption in the Strait of Hormuz could push oil and petrol prices higher, add to US inflation and become a political problem before the US midterm elections in November. That gives Tehran an obvious date to watch, but relying on American elections is a gamble.Iran's economy could be much weaker by then. And beyond the midterms lies another problem. With Trump not seeking re-election in 2028, his outgoing administration may feel it has more freedom to continue the confrontation with Iran and accept the costs.Iran is, therefore, watching two clocks.One is political and runs in Washington. The other is economic and runs inside Iran. Every month of lower oil exports, disrupted trade and pressure on the rial makes waiting for a deal to end the war more expensive.That leaves Iranian leaders with a difficult choice. Making concessions now could look like surrendering under pressure and strengthen hardliners who say Washington will only demand more.Waiting could improve Iran's position if Trump's strategy runs into political or economic problems. But Tehran could also find itself negotiating later with a weaker economy.Much now depends on what happens outside Iran.If Chinese banks, regional trading partners and companies start pulling back because they believe Washington will punish them, Bessent's campaign may change Tehran's calculation.If they do not, the opposite could happen. Those Iranians arguing against compromise will say Washington has played another supposedly decisive card without changing the balance and that Iran should continue to wait or resist.

schema.headline: Trump hopes sanctions will topple Iran's regime - its leaders are betting otherwise
